editorialSections.title: "Just train the team on ChatGPT." Watch that answer collapse.
editorialSections.eyebrow: The Ownership Gap · governance vs. vibes

blocks.text: The default reflex is to buy licenses and run a lunch-and-learn. That treats AI as a tooling problem. It's an ownership problem. Same situation, two responses: the generic training-first reflex, and the governance-grounded read that a Fractional CAO actually delivers. The distance between them is where the risk lives.
✕ Generic reflex · tool-first
"We should take AI seriously — let's train everyone on ChatGPT and see what sticks."
"Roll out licenses, run a training, encourage experimentation. Adoption will follow and we'll figure out policy later."
Feels like progress. Leaves four holes open — no one owns adoption, no one owns risk, there's no policy, and vendor/data governance is nobody's job. "Later" is when the incident happens.
✓ Aloha AI · governance-grounded NIST · ISO 42001
Same situation, read as governance:

Training is one lever of four, and not the first. Before adoption, someone has to own the decision: set the strategy, name accountability, and stand up the guardrails. Frameworks are explicit about this. NIST AI RMF makes Govern the cross-cutting function that holds the rest together; ISO/IEC 42001 puts AI oversight on top management, not the training calendar.

So the real read covers four fronts at once: adoption (who uses it, how, measured), risk ownership (who's accountable when it's wrong), policy (an actual AI policy, not a memo), and vendor governance (what data leaves, to whom, under what terms).

Confidence: High on the framework mapping, with legal applicability dependent on jurisdiction, system classification, role, and date. Each front maps to a named NIST AI RMF function, EU AI Act provision, or ISO/IEC 42001 control area in the method ledger below.
The Ownership Gap is the distance between having AI tools and having someone who owns them: strategy, governance, adoption, and risk. Training closes none of it. A Fractional CAO closes all of it.

editorialSections.title: Assess → Govern → Run: a repeatable strategy method

blocks.text: A Fractional CAO engagement isn't a slide deck. It's the same three-stage pipeline every time, adapted from regulatory monitoring to strategy: read the ground truth, resolve it into governance, then run it.
Assess: Readiness Intelligence Layer (RIL)

Ground truth first: current AI use, shadow tools, data flows, existing policy (or its absence), and where accountability actually sits. Scored against NIST AI RMF, the EU AI Act, and ISO/IEC 42001, not against a vendor's checklist.
Govern: Resolve to an Ownership Layer (ROL)

The assessment becomes decisions leadership can act on: a written strategy, an AI policy, a named oversight structure, vendor and data-handling guardrails, and a prioritized adoption plan. The gaps close in an order that matches your risk, not alphabetically.
Run: ongoing fractional ownership

Someone holds the mandate on a recurring cadence: driving adoption, keeping governance current as tools and rules shift, and answering to the board. From 2 days/week to full ownership, so it never goes leaderless again.

editorialSections.title: Every readiness dimension, grounded in a real framework

blocks.text: The scorecard's six dimensions aren't invented. Each maps to a named duty in a recognized AI-governance framework. Each entry carries its mechanism, the real source, a retrieval date, and a confidence rating, so the read holds up in a board conversation and in diligence.

cells.text: Governance & ownership as a cross-cutting duty: culture, policies, roles, accountability, and oversight that hold strategy, adoption, and risk together
NIST AI RMF 1.0 (NIST AI 100-1), Govern function of the Core
Risk ownership & measured management: mapping AI context and measuring/managing risk across the lifecycle, resourced by the govern function
NIST AI RMF 1.0, Map · Measure · Manage functions
Top-management accountability: AI oversight as leadership's responsibility, with an AI policy and objectives tied to strategic direction (not delegated to a training calendar)
Documented risk management, data governance, and human oversight as standing obligations for higher-risk AI use
EU AI Act (Reg. 2024/1689), Art. 9 (risk management) · Art. 26 (deployer obligations)
Adoption readiness: staff AI-literacy as an explicit organizational obligation, not an optional perk
EU AI Act (Reg. 2024/1689), Art. 4 — AI literacy (in application since Feb 2, 2025)
Data & vendor governance: third-party AI systems, datasets, and services as an in-scope governance concern, with lifecycle and supplier oversight
NIST AI RMF 1.0 (Govern, third-party risk) · ISO/IEC 42001:2023 (supplier oversight)

blocks.text: Verification checkpoint: NIST AI RMF 1.0 is voluntary guidance. Under the EU AI Act, prohibited-practice and AI-literacy provisions have applied since February 2, 2025, while the July 2026 AI Omnibus moved major high-risk-system obligations to December 2, 2027 for Annex III systems and August 2, 2028 for Annex I product systems. Other provisions follow their own dates. ISO/IEC 42001 is a certifiable management-system standard. Confirm jurisdiction, role, system classification, and the current consolidated law before treating any provision as binding. This is not legal advice.
